title: 5 Things Your Starter Is Telling You

slides.heading: Hooch (dark liquid on top)
slides.body: Your starter ran out of food and is begging for a feeding. Pour it off or stir it back in, then feed immediately.

slides.heading: Nail polish remover smell
slides.body: That acetone scent means acetic acid is running wild from hunger. Two to three proper feedings and it clears right up.

slides.heading: Bubbles but no rise
slides.body: Fermentation is happening but the gluten is too weak to trap gas. Switch to bread flour and check your hydration.

slides.heading: The Day 3 crash
slides.body: Your starter spiked on Day 2, then went flat. The initial bacteria are dying off so the real sourdough microbes can move in. Keep feeding.

slides.heading: Cheese or funky smells (week 1)
slides.body: Totally normal in the first 7 days. Unpleasant bacteria dominate early but cannot survive the rising acidity. They will be gone soon.

title: 5 Mistakes Ruining Your First Loaf

slides.heading: Using an immature starter
slides.body: A week-old starter with a few bubbles is not ready. Wait until it reliably doubles in 4-8 hours and passes the float test.

slides.heading: Under-fermenting the bulk
slides.body: This is the number one beginner error. Wait for a 50% volume increase, visible bubbles, and a jiggly, airy texture before shaping.

slides.heading: Weak shaping
slides.body: Without surface tension, your loaf spreads sideways instead of springing up. Pull the dough toward you on the counter to build a taut skin.

slides.heading: Not preheating long enough
slides.body: Your Dutch oven needs 45 minutes at max heat, minimum. Anything less means weak oven spring and a pale crust.

slides.heading: Cutting too early
slides.body: The bread is still cooking inside after it leaves the oven. Wait at least one hour or you will get a gummy crumb you will blame on under-baking.

title: Temperature: The Secret Control You're Ignoring

slides.heading: Warm zone (26-28C)
slides.body: The sweet spot for balanced fermentation. Both yeast and bacteria are happy, giving you a predictable peak and mildly tangy flavor.

slides.heading: Cool zone (20-22C)
slides.body: Fermentation slows way down, but acetic acid bacteria take the lead. This is how you get that sharp, San Francisco-style tang.

slides.heading: Cold zone (3-5C, the fridge)
slides.body: Nearly halts fermentation. Perfect for storing your starter between feedings or cold-proofing dough for incredible flavor.

slides.heading: The danger zone (above 35C)
slides.body: Yeast starts struggling here and dies at 40-45C. Direct sunlight and warm stovetops are starter killers.

slides.heading: Your kitchen has microclimates
slides.body: The spot on top of the fridge, near the oven, or by a window can vary by 9 degrees. Map them and use them strategically.

title: Hydration Demystified in 5 Slides

slides.heading: The formula is simple
slides.body: Hydration % = (water weight / flour weight) x 100. Equal parts flour and water = 100% hydration. That is the entire concept.

slides.heading: 100% = pancake batter
slides.body: Pourable, easy to stir, vigorous bubbling on the surface. The most common maintenance hydration because it is simple and readable.

slides.heading: 80% = thick oatmeal
slides.body: You scoop it, not pour it. Fermentation slows slightly and the flavor balance shifts toward a more complex tang.

slides.heading: 60% = a firm dough ball
slides.body: Mix it with your hands. Ferments very slowly over 10-16 hours and produces noticeably sharper, more vinegary bread.

slides.heading: Hydration controls flavor
slides.body: Warm and wet = mild, creamy sourness. Cool and stiff = sharp, assertive tang. You are literally dialing in flavor with water.

title: How to Nail the Perfect Peak Every Time

slides.heading: Volume: has it doubled?
slides.body: Mark the level with a rubber band right after feeding. A healthy starter at peak has at least doubled from that mark.

slides.heading: The dome test
slides.body: At peak, the surface is gently domed, rising in the center. Flat means you are at peak. Sinking means you are past it.

slides.heading: The jiggle test
slides.body: Tap the side of your jar. At peak, the starter jiggles like soft gelatin, bouncy and airy. After peak, it jiggles loosely and watery.

slides.heading: Aroma check
slides.body: Peak smells pleasantly tangy with a yeasty sweetness. If it smells like nail polish remover or booze, you missed the window.

slides.heading: The float test
slides.body: Drop a spoonful into water. If it floats, your starter is full of gas and likely at peak. Useful but not the only indicator you should rely on.

title: Feeding Ratios Cheat Sheet

slides.heading: 1:1:1 The Fast Build
slides.body: Equal parts everything. Peaks in 3-4 hours. Use this when you need to quickly build volume for a big bake.

slides.heading: 1:2:2 The Pre-Bake Feed
slides.body: Peaks in 4-6 hours, giving you a comfortable window. The go-to ratio when you want to bake the same day.

slides.heading: 1:5:5 Daily Maintenance
slides.body: Slow, balanced fermentation over 8-12 hours. Fits a once-a-day schedule and produces the most predictable results.

slides.heading: 1:5:3 Stiff Starter
slides.body: 60% hydration, dough-like consistency. Peaks in 10-16 hours with more acetic acid for a tangier, more complex bread.

slides.heading: Always weigh, never guess
slides.body: A cup of flour can vary by 30% depending on how you scoop it. A basic kitchen scale is the most important tool you own.

title: Your Starter Changes Every Season

slides.heading: Spring: The awakening
slides.body: Your starter speeds up as temps rise. Peaks that took 14 hours in January now arrive in 10. Adjust your timing before it runs away.

slides.heading: Summer: The sprint
slides.body: Everything goes into overdrive above 25C. Switch to 1:5:5 ratios and cool water. The fridge becomes your best tool.

slides.heading: Autumn: The golden season
slides.body: Ideal temps around 21-25C make fermentation predictable. This is when your best bread happens and the time to experiment.

slides.heading: Winter: The long game
slides.body: Cold kitchens mean 16+ hour peaks. Use warm water (28-32C), find a warm spot, and drop your ratio to 1:2:2 or 1:3:3.

slides.heading: One rule for every season
slides.body: Watch the dough, not the clock. Visual and aromatic cues are your real timer. The clock lies when your kitchen temperature changes.

title: Stop Throwing Away Your Discard

slides.heading: Discard is not garbage
slides.body: That starter you remove before feeding is full of flavor and ready to use in dozens of recipes. Zero-waste sourdough is real.

slides.heading: Discard pancakes
slides.body: Mix discard with eggs, milk, a touch of sugar, and baking soda. You get fluffy pancakes with a subtle tang that buttermilk ones cannot match.

slides.heading: Sourdough crackers
slides.body: Roll discard thin with olive oil, salt, and your favorite seasonings. Bake until crisp. They keep for weeks and beat anything store-bought.

slides.heading: Pizza dough and flatbreads
slides.body: Discard makes incredible pizza crusts and quick flatbreads. Even over-fermented dough works beautifully here.

slides.heading: Any discard works
slides.body: Fresh discard, week-old fridge discard, even slightly over-fermented stuff. The tangier it is, the more complex the flavor.

title: Not All Flour Is the Same

slides.heading: Bread flour (11-13% protein)
slides.body: The workhorse of sourdough. Strong gluten means tall, open-crumbed loaves with excellent oven spring. Start here.

slides.heading: Whole wheat (13-14% protein)
slides.body: Nutty, earthy, and fast-fermenting. The bran cuts through gluten strands, so blend 20-30% with bread flour for the best balance.

slides.heading: Rye (8-10% protein)
slides.body: The fermentation accelerator. Even 10% rye can jumpstart a sluggish starter. Deep, malty flavor with no gluten structure of its own.

slides.heading: All-purpose (9-11% protein)
slides.body: Lower protein means softer crumb and less spring. Great for discard recipes like pancakes and crackers, but not ideal for boules.

slides.heading: Check the protein number
slides.body: Two bags labeled 'bread flour' can differ by 2% in protein, which changes dough behavior completely. Always check the label.

title: Score Like a Pro: 5 Patterns to Try

slides.heading: The single slash (beginner)
slides.body: One confident cut at a 30-degree angle, slightly off-center. This is what creates the coveted ear. Master this one first.

slides.heading: The cross score (beginner)
slides.body: Two perpendicular vertical cuts forming a plus sign. Produces a rustic farmhouse look with four petals pulling apart evenly.

slides.heading: The wheat stalk (intermediate)
slides.body: A center line with short diagonal cuts branching off alternately. Stunning to look at but purely decorative, so add a functional cut too.

slides.heading: The spiral (advanced)
slides.body: A continuous curved line spiraling outward from the center. The whole surface unfurls like a pinwheel when it bakes.

slides.heading: Score cold dough only
slides.body: Score straight from the fridge. Cold dough holds its shape under the blade and gives dramatically cleaner cuts every single time.

title: You Can Control How Sour Your Bread Tastes

slides.heading: Two acids, two flavors
slides.body: Lactic acid is smooth and creamy like yogurt. Acetic acid is sharp and vinegary. The ratio between them is your master flavor dial.

slides.heading: Want milder bread?
slides.body: Ferment warm (25-30C), keep hydration high, use a young starter at peak, and do a shorter bulk fermentation.

slides.heading: Want tangier bread?
slides.body: Ferment cooler (18-22C), use a stiffer starter, extend the cold proof to 24-48 hours, and let the bulk go longer.

slides.heading: Cold proofing is the power move
slides.body: An overnight fridge proof develops flavor compounds that fast, warm fermentation simply cannot produce. Never skip it.

slides.heading: Salt amplifies everything
slides.body: At 2% of flour weight, salt controls fermentation and amplifies all other flavors. Under-salted bread tastes flat no matter what.

title: Why Your Loaf Keeps Going Flat

slides.heading: Surface tension is everything
slides.body: Without it, your loaf spreads sideways in the oven instead of springing up. The taut skin on top is what holds the shape together.

slides.heading: Pre-shape first, then rest
slides.body: Gather the dough into a rough ball, then leave it alone for 15-20 minutes. The gluten relaxes and becomes cooperative for final shaping.

slides.heading: Shape on an unfloured surface
slides.body: It sounds backwards, but friction between dough and countertop is what creates tension. Flour eliminates that friction.

slides.heading: Pull toward you gently
slides.body: Cup your hands behind the dough and drag it toward you. The bottom grips the surface while the top stretches taut. Rotate and repeat.

slides.heading: If it tears, you went too far
slides.body: Let the dough rest 5 minutes and do one more gentle pass. Practice is the only way to find the sweet spot.

title: The Only 5 Things You Need to Start

slides.heading: A digital kitchen scale
slides.body: Volume measurements can vary by 30%. A scale accurate to 1 gram costs under $15 and is the single most important tool in sourdough.

slides.heading: A clear glass jar
slides.body: You need to see what your starter is doing. Tall, straight-sided, wide-mouth. A cleaned pasta sauce jar works perfectly.

slides.heading: A rubber band or marker
slides.body: Place it at the starter level right after feeding. This is how you measure rise. Without it, you are completely guessing.

slides.heading: A large mixing bowl
slides.body: Glass or stainless steel, 4-5 liters. Wide and shallow for easy stretch and folds. It does not need to be fancy.

slides.heading: A Dutch oven with lid
slides.body: The game-changer for home bakers. It traps steam for oven spring and gives you a professional-quality crust. Even a stockpot with a lid works.

title: Sourdough Fits Your Life (Pick Your Schedule)

slides.heading: Total hands-on time: 30 minutes
slides.body: That is it. The rest is waiting. Sourdough takes 18 hours to exist but only half an hour of your actual attention.

slides.heading: The Weekend Baker
slides.body: Feed Thursday night. Mix Friday afternoon. Shape Friday evening. Cold proof overnight. Bake Saturday morning. Fresh bread for the weekend.

slides.heading: The 9-to-5 Baker
slides.body: Feed before work. Mix when you get home. Stretch and fold during dinner. Shape at bedtime. Bake the next morning before leaving.

slides.heading: The Busy Parent
slides.body: Mix whenever. Do stretch and folds when you walk through the kitchen. Fridge the dough. Shape tomorrow. Bake whenever. It all works.

slides.heading: The fridge is your pause button
slides.body: If life interrupts at any point, put the dough in the fridge. It holds for 12-36 hours cold. Resume when you are ready.

title: The Overnight Cold Proof Changes Everything

slides.heading: It is not just for convenience
slides.body: Cold proofing develops flavor compounds that fast, warm fermentation cannot create. Professional bakeries cold-proof every single loaf.

slides.heading: 12 hours = mild and balanced
slides.body: A standard overnight proof produces clean sourdough flavor with good complexity and an open crumb.

slides.heading: 24 hours = noticeable sourness
slides.body: Push it a full day and you get deeper tang, richer wheat notes, and a crust that caramelizes more beautifully.

slides.heading: 36+ hours = boldly tangy
slides.body: For the sharp, assertive sourdough lovers. Extended cold time lets acetic acid bacteria do their thing.

slides.heading: Cold dough scores better
slides.body: Scoring straight from the fridge is dramatically easier. The cold firms the surface so your blade glides cleanly instead of dragging.

title: Your First 7 Days: What to Expect

slides.heading: Days 1-2: Almost nothing
slides.body: Maybe a few bubbles by evening. It smells like wet flour. Some starters take 48 hours before anything visible happens. This is normal.

slides.heading: Day 3: The first feeding
slides.body: Discard half, feed with fresh flour and water. You may see a dramatic rise then a crash. That crash is progress, not failure.

slides.heading: Days 4-5: Signs of real life
slides.body: More consistent bubbling. The smell shifts from funky to tangy. The texture becomes stretchy when you stir. Things are happening.

slides.heading: Day 6: Gaining rhythm
slides.body: Your starter rises and falls predictably. You can see the pattern forming. If it peaks too fast, increase the flour ratio slightly.

slides.heading: Day 7: The float test
slides.body: At peak, drop a spoonful in water. If it floats, you may be ready. If not, keep feeding for a few more days. No two starters are the same.

title: Is That Mold or Hooch? (How to Tell)

slides.heading: Hooch = dark liquid on top
slides.body: Gray, brown, or black liquid is alcohol and water produced by hungry yeast. It is harmless. Pour it off or stir it in for extra tang.

slides.heading: Mold = fuzzy spots
slides.body: Actual mold looks fuzzy, not liquid. White, green, black, or pink fuzzy growths on the surface are a real problem.

slides.heading: Hooch means feed me
slides.body: Your starter consumed all its food and is sending a distress signal. Feed immediately and consider increasing your ratio.

slides.heading: When to start over
slides.body: Green, black, or pink mold means discard everything. Sterilize your jar. These organisms should not be in your culture.

slides.heading: Dark color is just oxidation
slides.body: A dark discoloration on top is almost always cosmetic. Stir it in, discard, feed, and the color returns to normal in 1-2 feeds.

title: Your Tap Water Might Be Killing Your Starter

slides.heading: Chlorine vs chloramine
slides.body: Both are added to kill microorganisms, which is exactly what you are trying to grow. Know which one your water has.

slides.heading: Chlorine is easy to fix
slides.body: Fill a jug and leave it uncovered on the counter overnight. By morning, the chlorine has evaporated. Free and simple.

slides.heading: Chloramine is trickier
slides.body: It does not evaporate. You need a carbon filter, or just use bottled spring water. Check your water utility website to find out which you have.

slides.heading: Skip distilled water
slides.body: It lacks the minerals that support fermentation. Your starter needs some mineral content to thrive.

slides.heading: Water temperature matters too
slides.body: Lukewarm water (25-28C) gives a gentle boost. Cold water stalls things. Water above 40C will straight up kill your yeast.

title: Stretch and Fold: The Technique That Replaces Kneading

slides.heading: Why stretch and fold?
slides.body: It builds gluten gently over time without the aggressive kneading that traditional bread demands. Four sets is all you need.

slides.heading: How to do it
slides.body: Wet your hand, slide it under one side, stretch up until resistance, fold over the center. Rotate 90 degrees. Repeat 4 times per set.

slides.heading: Space them 30 minutes apart
slides.body: Four sets over two hours, each taking less than a minute. The dough transforms from slack and sticky to smooth and elastic.

slides.heading: You will feel the change
slides.body: Set 1 feels like wrestling wet clay. By Set 4, the dough is cohesive, springy, and holds its shape. That is gluten developing.

slides.heading: After folds: hands off
slides.body: Once your four sets are done, cover the bowl and let bulk fermentation do its work. The yeast and bacteria handle the rest.

cta: Practice this weekend!

title: How to Know When Bulk Fermentation Is Done

slides.heading: Look for 50% volume increase
slides.body: Not double. Just 50% bigger than when you started. Going to double is usually too far for most home kitchen temperatures.

slides.heading: The jiggle test
slides.body: Nudge the bowl gently. Ready dough feels airy and jiggles like a water balloon. Stiff means more time. Slack and soupy means too far.

slides.heading: Bubbles on surface and edges
slides.body: You should see bubbles forming around the sides of the bowl and dotting the surface. No bubbles means more time is needed.

slides.heading: The poke test
slides.body: Press a floured finger gently into the dough. It should spring back slowly with a slight indentation. Instant spring-back means keep waiting.

slides.heading: Watch the dough, not the clock
slides.body: A warm kitchen finishes in 3 hours. A cool kitchen takes 5+. Visual and tactile cues are always more reliable than a timer.

title: Going on Vacation? Your Starter Will Survive

slides.heading: 1-2 weeks: just fridge it
slides.body: Give it a big feed at 1:10:10, cap loosely, and refrigerate. Revive with 2-3 feedings when you return.

slides.heading: 2-4 weeks: stiff feed + fridge
slides.body: Feed with a high ratio and refrigerate. It may look ugly when you get back. Hooch, grey color, strong smell. All normal.

slides.heading: Months or years: dry it
slides.body: Spread active starter thin on parchment paper. Let it dry completely. Break into flakes and store in an airtight jar. Revives with flour and water.

slides.heading: The two-jar rule
slides.body: Keep a backup jar in the fridge, fed every two weeks. If your main starter gets contaminated or tossed, you have insurance.

slides.heading: Starters are survivors
slides.body: They have endured for thousands of years through famines and neglect. Your two-week beach trip is nothing.

title: The Invisible World Living in Your Starter

slides.heading: It is a partnership
slides.body: Wild yeast makes your bread rise. Lactic acid bacteria create the flavor and protect the ecosystem. They literally feed each other.

slides.heading: The metabolic handshake
slides.body: Bacteria break down maltose and release glucose. Yeast eats that glucose. In return, acid from bacteria creates an environment only they can survive in.

slides.heading: A four-act feeding cycle
slides.body: Act 1: Fresh food arrives. Act 2: Microbes multiply. Act 3: Peak gas production. Act 4: Food runs out, everything slows.

slides.heading: Self-regulating ecosystem
slides.body: The acid produced keeps mold and harmful bacteria out. Once established, your starter resists invasion. It is remarkably stable.

slides.heading: Every starter is local
slides.body: Your flour, water, kitchen, and schedule create a unique microbial fingerprint. Two identical routines in different cities produce different bread.

title: Why You MUST Discard Before Feeding

slides.heading: It is about math
slides.body: Without discarding, you double your flour and water each feeding. By Day 7, you would have 6+ kilograms of starter.

slides.heading: No discard starves everyone
slides.body: The microbe population grows but food per organism shrinks. Acid builds up before yeast can do its job.

slides.heading: Discarding resets the ratio
slides.body: Removing old culture ensures the remaining organisms have plenty of fresh food for a full fermentation cycle.

slides.heading: It keeps the right microbes in charge
slides.body: A proper feeding ratio gives yeast and bacteria enough buffer before acid levels become inhibitory.

slides.heading: Your discard has a second life
slides.body: Pancakes, crackers, waffles, pizza dough, flatbreads. Nothing goes to waste unless you choose to waste it.
